id: Body of Rags, International Bridge Between the US & Mexico

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Is it alive? —neither a head, legs nor arms! ................... ... torpid against the flange of the supporting girder . ? an inhuman shapelessness, knees hugged tight up into the belly Egg-shaped! —William Carlos Williams, 1950 visit to El Paso, from “Desert Music” Yes, I am a body of rags lying here on the bridge waiting for a hot rain to wash me open, dissolve me off the bridge because this border is closed. I rot on the boundary line and can’t enter Juarez, pennies thrown at me when a drunk El Pasoan returns in the darkness and sees my shape that makes him hurry across. No head, decades ago they threw it in the river without my screams. My arms were the first to go when I couldn’t climb the wall. I can never leave this bridge. I live on the pure line that divides countries and grabs my hunger from sliding into Mexico with my outstretched hands. I still have my knees. I used to be sold in Juarez and smuggled into El Paso, the egg that floated down the Rio Grande to break hundreds of miles away before being thrown back. I stay on the bridge and can’t move. Do not cross to El Paso without wiping your shoes of me, one foot on US concrete, the other scraping away at my Mexican rags. When I struggle against the wire fence, I make sure I salute two flags.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The poem responds to William Carlos Williams' 1950 description of a shapeless, torpid figure witnessed in El Paso, reimagining it as a symbolic border-dweller. - The speaker embodies a dismembered, bodiless figure—lacking head and arms—that exists permanently trapped on the bridge between El Paso and Juarez. - This liminal being represents the immigrant condition, unable to fully enter either the United States or Mexico, rotting on the boundary line between nations. - The poem uses physical fragmentation (lost head, missing arms, remaining knees) as a metaphor for the violence and dehumanization inflicted upon those caught in border limbo. - The closing imagery of saluting "two flags" while scraping shoes on both nations' soil underscores the divided, dual identity forced upon those who inhabit this contested threshold space.
prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

This poem, responding to William Carlos Williams' 1950 depiction of a dehumanized, shapeless figure on the El Paso-Juárez border, gives voice to that formless body through first-person narration, transforming an object of pity into a speaking subject trapped between nations. The poem reveals how border violence literally dismembers identity—stripping away head, arms, and mobility—while the figure's endurance on the dividing line itself becomes a haunting testament to the human cost of geopolitical boundaries and the impossibility of belonging fully to either country.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Egg, William, Carlos

outputs.L1:
# Refined Version

*Is it alive?*
*—neither a head, legs nor arms!*
*...................*
*...*
*torpid against the flange of the supporting girder*
*.*
*?*
*an inhuman shapelessness, knees hugged tight up into the belly*
*Egg-shaped!*

—William Carlos Williams, 1950 visit to El Paso, from "Desert Music"

Yes, I am a body of rags,
lying here upon the bridge,
waiting for a hot rain
to wash me open, to dissolve me
from this bridge—
because the border is closed.

I rot along the boundary line,
unable to enter Juárez,
pennies flung at me
when some drunken El Pasoan,
returning through the dark,
glimpses my shape
and quickens his pace across.

No head—decades ago
they cast it into the river
without my screaming.
My arms were the first to go,
when I could not scale the wall.
I can never leave this bridge.

I exist upon the very line
that divides two nations,
clutching my hunger back
from sliding into Mexico
with outstretched hands.

I still have my knees.
Once I was sold in Juárez,
smuggled into El Paso—
the egg that drifted down the Rio Grande,
cracking hundreds of miles from home
before being cast back again.

I remain upon this bridge,
unable to move.

Do not cross into El Paso
without first wiping your shoes clean of me—
one foot upon American concrete,
the other scraping free
my Mexican rags.

And when I struggle against the wire fence,
I make certain
I salute both flags.
outputs.L2:
# Rewritten Version

Is it living? —no head, no legs, no arms to speak of! ................... ... numb where it rests against the girder's edge . ? a shape too strange to be human, knees drawn up tight against its belly Like an egg! —William Carlos Williams, 1950 visit to El Paso, from "Desert Music"

Indeed, I am nothing but a heap of rags stretched across this bridge, hoping for scalding rain to dissolve me, to wash what remains of me from this crossing, because the border stands sealed. I decay along this dividing line, forbidden from reaching Juarez, coins tossed my way whenever some intoxicated El Pasoan stumbles back through the night, catches sight of my form, and quickens his pace to escape.

My head vanished long ago, cast into the river without hearing my cries. My arms were lost first, back when scaling the wall proved impossible. This bridge has become my permanent prison. I exist upon the exact border separating two nations, my reaching hands preventing my starvation from slipping across into Mexican territory.

My knees, at least, remain intact. Once I was traded in Juarez, then smuggled across into El Paso—an egg carried by the Rio Grande's current, destined to shatter countless miles from home before being cast back to where I began. Trapped on this bridge, I cannot budge an inch.

Never cross into El Paso without first scraping me from your soles—plant one foot on American pavement while the other grinds away at my Mexican remnants. Whenever I thrash against the border fence, I make certain to honor both flags simultaneously.
outputs.L3:
# The Body at the Border: A Meditation on Liminal Existence

This poem enters into dialogue with William Carlos Williams' 1950 observation—a brief but haunting description of a shapeless, torpid figure he witnessed in El Paso. Rather than simply recounting this historical moment, the poem transforms Williams' fleeting image into something far more resonant: a symbolic embodiment of the border-dweller, someone whose existence is defined entirely by the space between nations rather than belonging to either one.

At the center of the poem stands a startling figure—the speaker themselves, rendered as dismembered and bodiless. Lacking a head to think or see clearly, missing arms that might reach toward either shore, this fragmented being exists in a state of permanent suspension, trapped physically and metaphorically on the bridge connecting El Paso and Ciudad Juárez. This is not a temporary crossing but an eternal condition, a body caught mid-transit with no possibility of arrival.

Through this haunting image, the poem articulates something essential about the immigrant experience: the impossibility of full belonging to either side of an arbitrary line. The figure cannot enter the United States, nor can it return whole to Mexico. Instead, it remains suspended, decomposing on the very boundary that defines and divides these two nations. This rotting is not merely physical but existential—a slow erasure of self that occurs when one is denied full citizenship or recognition in any single place.

The poem's use of bodily fragmentation—the absent head, the missing arms, the lone knees that somehow remain—functions as a powerful metaphor for the violence inherent in border existence. To lose one's head suggests a loss of voice, of rational agency, of the ability to be seen as fully human. To lose one's arms implies an inability to labor, to embrace, to defend oneself, or to reach toward connection. What remains—mere knees—suggests only the capacity for supplication, for kneeling, for a diminished physical presence that echoes the dehumanization so often inflicted upon those caught in the limbo of border crossing. This is a body reduced to fragments by systems of control, surveillance, and exclusion that transform whole persons into partial, spectral remnants.

The poem's closing image proves especially potent: this fragmented figure saluting "two flags" while scraping its shoes against the soil of both nations. This gesture captures the impossible duality demanded of those who inhabit border spaces—an enforced allegiance to two nations simultaneously, neither of which fully claims or accepts them. The scraping of shoes against both soils suggests both an attempt at grounding and a perpetual restlessness, a body trying to root itself in two places at once yet belonging fully to neither. This final image crystallizes the poem's central tension: the border-dweller as a figure of divided loyalty and fractured identity, forever performing citizenship to two flags while truly possessing a home in neither.
outputs.L4:
# Between Two Rivers: A Response

In 1950, William Carlos Williams stood at the threshold of El Paso and Juárez and witnessed something that troubled him deeply enough to commit it to verse: a figure so broken by circumstance, so worn down by the machinery of border existence, that it had become nearly shapeless—a mass of suffering rather than a person. Williams, ever the physician-poet, observed with clinical precision but from the outside, rendering this figure as an object of contemplation, a symbol of the border's cruelty, but ultimately voiceless. The body became a kind of specimen, pitiable but silent, unable to speak for itself across the seven decades that would separate its creation from this poetic response.

This new poem undertakes a radical act of reclamation: it seizes the first-person voice and hands it back to that formless body. Where Williams observed, this poem inhabits. Where the original rendered the figure as a shape to be pitied from a comfortable distance, this response insists on interiority—on the possibility that even a body stripped of its wholeness retains consciousness, memory, and the capacity for testimony. The transformation is not merely stylistic but political: an object becomes a subject, a symbol becomes a self.

The poem's central metaphor operates with brutal literalism. Border violence, it suggests, does not merely wound or traumatize—it dismembers. The head disappears, taking with it the capacity for recognized personhood, for the face that grants humanity in official documents and social recognition. The arms vanish, stripping away agency, the ability to reach toward one nation or the other, to grasp at belonging. Mobility itself becomes impossible; the figure cannot walk toward citizenship, cannot cross fully into either identity. What remains is a torso, a trunk, a core of suffering that persists precisely because it has nowhere else to go.

This dismemberment is not merely metaphorical excess but a precise accounting of what the border does to those caught within its liminal space. The nation-state's violence operates through bureaucratic and physical mechanisms that quite literally fragment identity: the undocumented worker who cannot claim full personhood in either country, the deported individual whose family remains divided by an arbitrary line, the border crosser whose body bears the marks of walls, fences, and enforcement. The poem insists that these are not abstract political categories but embodied realities—that the border inscribes itself upon flesh.

Yet the figure endures. This endurance becomes the poem's most haunting achievement. Positioned literally upon the dividing line—not in El Paso, not in Juárez, but in the contested, ambiguous space between—the speaker exists in a state of perpetual liminality. This is not belonging to two worlds but exile from both, a condition of permanent in-betweenness that the poem refuses to resolve or redeem. The dividing line itself becomes a kind of home, though a home that is no home at all—a space defined entirely by its function as boundary, as separation, as the mark of exclusion rather than inclusion.

In giving voice to Williams' original figure, the poem performs a kind of resurrection, but one that does not restore wholeness. The speaking subject remains fragmented, headless and armless in the metaphorical sense even as it gains the capacity for speech. This paradox—a voice emerging from a body that cannot fully move or fully see—becomes the poem's central meditation on the human cost of geopolitical boundaries. It suggests that even language, even testimony, even the first-person "I" cannot fully restore what borders have taken away. The poem thus stands as both tribute to and departure from Williams' original vision: where he offered witness from outside, this poem offers testimony from within, insisting that even the most dehumanized figures retain something that must be heard, must be reckoned with, must be understood as fundamentally, irreducibly human despite—or perhaps because of—everything that has been stripped away.
outputs.L5:
# The Egg Contest

William had never taken cooking seriously until his neighbor Carlos challenged him to a friendly competition: who could make the most creative dish using only eggs as the main ingredient.

"You're on," William said, grinning with more confidence than skill.

The following Saturday, both men set up makeshift stations in Carlos's backyard. William arrived with a dozen eggs, a bag of spinach, and an ambitious idea for a soufflé. Carlos, on the other hand, brought ingredients for a traditional Spanish tortilla, a recipe passed down from his grandmother in Seville.

As the afternoon progressed, William's soufflé rose beautifully in the oven, filling the yard with a savory aroma. Meanwhile, Carlos worked methodically, slicing potatoes thin and folding them gently into beaten eggs, his movements practiced and sure.

When the timer went off, William pulled his creation from the oven with pride—only to watch it deflate slightly as he set it down. Carlos chuckled sympathetically. "Happens to the best of us," he said, flipping his tortilla with a confident flick of the wrist.

In the end, both dishes were delicious in their own way. William's soufflé, though slightly fallen, tasted rich and flavorful. Carlos's tortilla was perfectly golden, tender in the center just as his grandmother had taught him.

They declared it a tie, sharing both dishes over cold beers as the sun set. William admitted he had a lot to learn, and Carlos offered to teach him more recipes passed down through his family.

What started as a lighthearted bet turned into a new tradition—every month, the two neighbors would gather to cook, swap stories, and celebrate the simple joy of turning humble ingredients like eggs into something memorable.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem that responds to William Carlos Williams' "The Desert Music," using the image of the shapeless figure on the bridge as a speaker who embodies the US-Mexico border experience.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Bridge Remembers**
*(after Williams, "The Desert Music")*

You saw me as a huddle, a rag-pile,
something the night left folded
on the concrete lip between your country
and the one that isn't quite mine either—

I was there before your poem found me,
before you asked *is it a bundle of rags*
and answered your own question
by walking closer, by needing to know.

I'll tell you now what I couldn't then:
I am shapeless because the shape
was taken from me at the middle
of the bridge, where the paint changes color,
where the flag on one side salutes
and the flag on the other side salutes
and I am the space between salutes.

The river below me forgot how to be a river.
It is a fence now, a green idea,
a number typed into a database.
I have crossed it so many times
in dreams that my feet no longer
remember which side made them tired.

Call me nothing if you must call me something—
I have been called nothing in two languages,
in the clipped Spanish of the checkpoint,
in the flat English of the form.
I have learned to answer to nothing
the way a dog learns its beaten name.

But listen: I breathe. I lie here breathing
under the sodium lights, under the stars
that don't require a visa,
and my breathing is the desert music
you were listening for all along—
not the mariachi trumpet, not the border patrol radio,
but this: the sound of a body
insisting it is a body,
here, on the bridge, at 2 a.m.,
neither arriving nor departed,
neither your rags nor your poem
but the thing itself, unresolved,
the shape that shape forgot,
singing without a mouth
*I am here, I am here, I am here.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a persona poem where the "egg-shaped" homeless figure from Williams' "Desert Music" speaks in first person about living on the border bridge between El Paso and Juarez.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Bridge Between

I am the shape they could not name—
egg-shaped, the poet called me,
curled like something not yet born
or something that has stopped becoming.

I lie where the river used to matter,
where the line on the map grows thin
and men in uniforms pretend
the dirt cares whose flag it wears.

By day I am a smudge in your peripheral vision,
a lump of shadow the sun forgets to burn away.
By night I am the bridge's secret organ,
pumping nothing, holding still,
between the two mouths of a country
that cannot decide which language
to spit me out in.

El Paso says: *not mine.*
Juárez says: *not mine.*
The river, what's left of it,
says nothing—
it has learned the wisdom of silence,
the way water does
when it has been told too many times
where it is allowed to run.

I have made my body a comma
in the long sentence of the border,
a pause between two clauses
that never resolve.

I do not remember choosing this curl,
this fetal geometry, this refusal
to stand up and be measured
by the metrics of your citizenship.
Maybe I was straight once.
Maybe the weight of two nations
pressing from either end of the bridge
bent me into this shape—
an egg, something waiting,
something that might yet crack open
into a life, or might just
harden here, calcified,
a fossil of the space between.

The tourists photograph me
without asking, the way you photograph
a strange rock formation, a curiosity
of geology. I am becoming
the terrain. I am becoming
what the bridge remembers
when it dreams: not steel, not payment,
not customs and inspections,
but this—a body
that belongs to no address,
that has made a home
of the exact place
where home is not allowed to be.

Listen: I do not speak your border Spanish
or your border English.
I speak bridge.
I speak the language of concrete
that has forgotten it was once
a promise between two cities
who used to be one river,
one silt, one bed
before the world got hungry
for its own edges.

I am the pulse beneath the tourists' feet,
the thing the music almost says
when Williams tried to sing me—
he saw the shape but not the ache,
the curve but not the years
it takes to fold a person
into punctuation,
into the small silence
that holds two languages apart
so they don't flood into each other
and become, God forbid,
something whole.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem that begins by quoting Williams' description of the strange shape on the bridge, then shifts into the voice of that figure, exploring themes of statelessness, mutilation, and border violence.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Shape on the Bridge

*"a strange shape... crouched, half-naked,
at the edge of the bridge"*
—so the report reads, so the officer writes it down,
a shape, not a man, not yet a name.

I was crouched because kneeling is what's left
when the legs remember running
but the feet have nowhere left to land.
Half-naked because the river took
the rest of me somewhere upstream—
my shirt, my papers, the language
I used to pray in.

Call me shape. It's easier
than calling me by what they did.

*

I had a country once.
It fit me like a second skin
until they peeled it off
to check what was underneath.
Turns out: nothing official.
Turns out: a body is not
a valid form of identification.

*

They found me at the border
the way you find a wound—
already there, already old,
waiting for someone to notice
the bleeding.

I am the crouch between two flags.
I am the sound a bridge makes
when it holds more weight
than it was built for—
all this history,
all this water underneath,
all these names
that don't appear
on any list.

*

Half-naked, they wrote.
As if a man could be measured
in percentages of cloth,
in fractions of a self
still recognizable.

I'll tell you what mutilation is:
it's a line drawn on a map
that goes through a man's chest
instead of around it.
It's a checkpoint
built on top of a heartbeat.
It's being asked for documents
by a fence that was once
your grandfather's field.

*

So yes—strange shape.
Yes—crouched, half-naked,
at the edge, at the edge,
always at the edge,
because the middle
was never meant for me,

because the bridge
is the only country
that will still hold me,

suspended,
between the last shore
that called me stranger
and the next one
that hasn't decided yet
what to call me
at all.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an ekphrastic/intertextual poem reacting to the opening lines of "The Desert Music," giving voice to the ambiguous body Williams describes, using surreal imagery of losing limbs and living permanently on the international bridge.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Bridge Keeps**

*after the opening of "The Desert Music"*

You saw me and could not decide —
rags, or a man, or the memory
of a man folded like a rag —
and I have let you wonder
because deciding is a border too
and I live on that one now.

I gave up my legs first.
They walked into the river
without me, kept going,
became two more cables
strung between the stanchions,
humming when trucks pass over.
I do not miss them. I did not
need to arrive anywhere.

My arms I lent to the railings.
Touch the rust and you are touching
what used to reach for things —
a woman's sleeve, a coin,
the shape of my own name.
Now they only hold the wind
in place a little longer
before it crosses without a visa.

I sleep in the seam
where the two floors of the world
almost meet and do not.
Not Juárez. Not El Paso.
Something the size of a heartbeat
wedged in the expansion joint,
swelling in the heat, shrinking
each cold, the way concrete does,
the way I do.

Officers pass over my ambiguity
the way light passes over a coin
face-down — they cannot tell
which country's profile
I've become, so they let me
be the bridge's shadow instead,
a plank of dark
folded the length of the railing,
that might sit up, might not,
might be the poem's excuse
to keep walking.

I am practicing the long patience
of things that are looked at
and then continued past.
Rags do this well. So do bodies
that have decided
which of their pieces
they can afford to lose
in order to stay exactly
here — neither arriving
nor departing, only
the small tremor
under the traveler's feet
that says *someone
has been living
in the crossing itself.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a poem in two parts: first cite Williams' 1950 observation of the shapeless figure at the El Paso-Juarez bridge, then have that figure narrate its own fragmented, border-crossing existence in stark, unsettling language.
counterfactuals.output:
**I. The Sighting**

Williams came to the bridge in 1950,
crossing from El Paso into Juárez,
the two names stitched by one long plank of concrete,
and there — against the rail, half in the road —
a heap. Not quite a man. Not quite a sack of laundry
left by someone who forgot they owned it.

He looked twice, the way a poet looks,
suspicious of his own eyes,
and wrote it down before deciding
whether it breathed.

*A bundle of rags*, he called it,
*a shapeless mass*,
and let the ambiguity stand
like a border itself —
not quite wall, not quite water,
a line drawn through dust
that somehow held two countries apart
by agreeing to touch nowhere at all.

He did not wake it.
He did not name it.
He let it lie there, unclaimed,
a comma in the long sentence
between one flag and another,
and walked on,
carrying the shape of it
the way you carry a smell
you can't place until later,
until it becomes a poem,
until it becomes this.

---

**II. What the Bundle Said**

I do not have a shape.
I have a location.

Here — no. Here — no.
The bridge keeps sliding
under the word *here.*

I am made of what was left over
after two governments
finished arguing about me.

Cloth. Dust. A number
someone wrote on paper
and then lost the paper.

I sleep in the direction
water sleeps —
downhill, downhill,
toward whichever river
will still have me.

Ask what I am
and I will answer in pieces:

a name half-said in Spanish,
a name half-said in English,
the silence between them
where the actual name used to live.

I have crossed so many times
the crossing crossed itself out.
Now I am only the residue
of arrival —

not arrived,
not left,
a shape a poet found
too true to sketch,
too human to ignore,
too unclaimed
to be anything
but exactly
what I am:

nobody's,
and therefore
everyone's,

lying at the seam
where the map
forgot to finish stitching,

waiting
not to be rescued
but to be
seen all the way through —

which is worse,
and which I have,
after all this time,
almost stopped
wanting.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
